extracted.intended_audience: advanced high-school and undergraduate math students / contest problem solvers
extracted.subtask_description: Expository textbook chapters giving definitions, theorems, examples, and problem prompts on duals/adjoints/transposes in linear algebra and on group actions, orbits, and Sylow theory in group theory (with olympiad/AIME style applications).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the dual map (T∨)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given linear T: V → W, the dual map T∨ : W∨ → V∨ is defined by T∨(f) = f ◦ T for f ∈ W∨.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a basis-free definition; in coordinates the matrix of T∨ (with respect to dual bases) is the transpose of the matrix of T. Example 15.1.2 computes T and T∨ in concrete bases to illustrate this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transpose interpretation of the dual map (Theorem 15.1.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: For finite-dimensional V, W and chosen bases (ei) for V and (fj) for W, the matrix of T in bases (ei),(fj) and the matrix of T∨ in bases (f∨j),(e∨i) are transposes of each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The (i,j)-entry of T is the coefficient of fi in T(ej); this corresponds to the coefficient of e∨j in f∨i ◦ T, giving the transpose relationship. Emphasizes that the dual map definition is basis-free and the transpose phenomenon holds in any chosen bases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Row rank equals column rank (Theorem 15.2.1 / Problem 15C)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an m×n matrix M over a field k, the column rank (dimension spanned by column vectors in k^m) equals the row rank (dimension spanned by row vectors in k^n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof can be approached via Theorem 9.7.6 and Theorem 15.1.3 (use dual map arguments). Also left as problems 15B and 15C; later sections provide basis-free proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution: non-canonical identification V ≅ V∨ can mislead
rubrics_metrics.description: Identifying V with V∨ by selecting a basis (ei ↦ e∨i) is not natural in general; using such a random isomorphism in proofs can produce incorrect statements (counterexamples over C).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A bogus proof is given that M⊤M and M have the same rank by implicitly using a random isomorphism ι: W → W∨; the fix over R is to choose ι(w)=⟨−,w⟩ with an orthonormal basis so that the intervening matrix becomes the identity. Exercise 15.2.2 exhibits a complex counterexample.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification V → V∨ via inner product for real spaces (Theorem 15.3.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a finite-dimensional real inner product space V, the map v ↦ ⟨−, v⟩ ∈ V∨ is an isomorphism of real vector spaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: show injectivity (use positive-definiteness) and surjectivity (map orthonormal basis vectors to dual basis). This gives a canonical identification in the real case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex inner product spaces: bijection but anti-linear (Theorem 15.3.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a finite-dimensional complex inner product space V, the map v ↦ ⟨−, v⟩ is a bijection of sets (injective and surjective) but is not C-linear; it is anti-linear (conjugate-linear).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: ⟨−, i v⟩ = −i ⟨−, v⟩ shows the map introduces conjugation, so it's not a complex-linear isomorphism. One can consider alternative fixes (Problem 15D) but the map remains anti-linear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the adjoint (conjugate transpose) T†
rubrics_metrics.description: For finite-dimensional inner product spaces V, W and linear T: V → W, the adjoint T†: W → V is defined by the property ⟨v, T†(w)⟩_V = ⟨T(v), w⟩_W for all v ∈ V and w ∈ W.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remarks: T† is well-defined because v ↦ ⟨T(v), w⟩_W is in V∨ and corresponds (via the inner-product identification) to a unique vector in V; T† is linear; definition is basis-free and thus the 'right' notion for inner product spaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjoints are conjugate transposes in orthonormal bases (Theorem 15.4.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an orthonormal basis is fixed, the matrix representing T† is the conjugate-transpose (Hermitian transpose) of the matrix for T: the (i,j)-entry of T† equals the complex conjugate of the (j,i)-entry of T.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof reduces to checking the defining equation on basis vectors. Example 15.4.2 shows how sesquilinearity conjugates coefficients (e.g., conjugating factors of i) when computing T† on basis vectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of normal and Hermitian (self-adjoint) maps (Definition 15.5.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A linear map T on a finite-dimensional inner product space is normal if T T† = T† T. It is Hermitian (self-adjoint) if T = T† (for real matrices: symmetric).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These definitions classify when orthonormal eigenbases exist and when eigenvalues are real (Hermitian case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization: normal ⇔ diagonalizable by orthonormal eigenbasis (Theorem 15.5.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: A linear map T on a finite-dimensional complex inner product space is normal iff there exists an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors (i.e., T is unitarily diagonalizable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof outlines: show ker T = ker T^r = ker T† for r ≥ 1 (Claim 15.5.4), argue no Jordan blocks of size >1, diagonalize, and show eigenvectors with distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal. Use Gram-Schmidt for repeated eigenvalues. Corollary: Hermitian matrices are diagonalizable with real eigenvalues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hermitian matrices have real eigenvalues (Theorem 15.5.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: If T = T† (Hermitian), then T is diagonalizable and all eigenvalues are real.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: Hermitian implies normal, diagonalize in orthonormal eigenbasis; equality T = T† forces each eigenvalue to equal its complex conjugate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonical double dual isomorphism (Problem 15A)
rubrics_metrics.description: For finite-dimensional V, the map V → (V∨)∨ given by v ↦ (ξ ↦ ξ(v)) is a canonical isomorphism (basis-independent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Significance: this isomorphism is canonical (does not depend on basis choice), unlike naive V ≅ V∨ identifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental theorem of linear algebra in dual form (Problem 15B)
rubrics_metrics.description: For T: V → W finite-dimensional over field k, dim im T = dim im T∨ = dim V − dim ker T = dim W − dim ker T∨.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relates ranks and nullities of T and its dual; useful in proofs like row rank = column rank.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of adjoint with dual in real inner product spaces (Problem 15E)
rubrics_metrics.description: For real inner product spaces V, W and linear T: V → W, the diagram relating T† and T∨ via the identifications v ↦ ⟨−, v⟩ commutes; hence T† corresponds to T∨ when duals are eliminated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows that in real inner-product settings the adjoint is simply the dual map under the canonical identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polynomial criterion for normality (Problem 15F)
rubrics_metrics.description: For finite-dimensional complex inner product space V and linear T: V → V, T is normal iff there exists a polynomial p ∈ C[t] such that T† = p(T).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret p(T) in the sense of polynomial functional calculus (composition), as in Cayley-Hamilton context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence of Kronecker product definitions (Problem 15G)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two viewpoints of the Kronecker product agree: (1) as A⊗B acting on tensor products V1⊗V2 by (v1⊗v2)↦A(v1)⊗B(v2), and (2) as the matrix operation sending a q×n matrix X to the p×m matrix B X A⊤ when A is m×n and B is p×q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem asks to reconcile the mathematician's tensor-product definition with the computer-scientist matrix-block definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rank equality M†M and M (Problem 15H)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an m×n complex matrix M, M† M and M have equal rank.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise suggests finding a basis-free proof; connected to identification of images/kernels under adjoint-related maps (use that ker S = ker T relationships for S = T†T).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a group action (Definition 16.1.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A group action of G on a set X is a map ·: G×X → X satisfying (g1 g2)·x = g1·(g2·x) and 1_G·x = x for all g1,g2 ∈ G and x ∈ X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prototypical examples: rotations acting on colorings of a board (AIME problem), permutations acting on {1,...,n}, left multiplication action of G on itself. Exercise 16.1.3: equivalently a group homomorphism G → S_X.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stabilizer definition and subgroup property (Definition 16.2.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: For x ∈ X, Stab_G(x) = {g ∈ G | g·x = x}; the stabilizer is a subgroup of G.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in the 7×7 board rotation problem, the configuration with two opposite yellow corners has stabilizer {1, r^2} ≅ Z/2Z. Exercise 16.2.4 asks to show Stab_G(x) is a subgroup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orbit-stabilizer theorem (Theorem 16.2.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an orbit O with representative x and stabilizer S = Stab_G(x), there is a bijection between O and the left cosets G/S, and |O| · |S| = |G|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the bijection gS ↦ g·x. Consequence: stabilizers of elements in the same orbit have equal size. Fundamental for counting orbit sizes and applying group actions to combinatorics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burnside's lemma (Theorem 16.3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For finite group G acting on finite set X, the number of orbits equals (1/|G|) ∑_{g∈G} |FixPt(g)| where FixPt(g) = {x ∈ X | g·x = x}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof deferred as an olympiad-style bonus; applied concretely to the AIME 1996 example: average fixed-coloring counts for group elements gave 300 inequivalent colorings. Use to count colorings modulo symmetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjugation action and conjugacy classes (Definition 16.4.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: G acts on itself by conjugation g: h ↦ g h g^{-1}. The conjugacy classes are the orbits of this action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example in S_n: conjugacy classes correspond to cycle type (shape) — two permutations are conjugate iff they have the same cycle structure. Related exercises: number of conjugacy classes equals number of partitions of n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Center of a group (Definition 16.4.5) and trivial conjugacy in abelian groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Z(G) = {x ∈ G | xg = gx for all g ∈ G}. In abelian groups every element commutes, so conjugacy classes are singletons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check Z(G) is a subgroup; question about why Z(G) is normal. Conjugacy classes of elements in the center are singletons by definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burnside/AIME-style counting examples and exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: Worked examples (AIME 1996) and exercises (e.g., MathCounts spinner) illustrate applying Burnside's lemma and orbit-stabilizer to count colorings/modulo symmetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete computation of |FixPt(g)| for each g in symmetry group and averaging; use these examples as templates for similar counting problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sylow theorems (Theorem 17.1.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For |G| = p^n m with gcd(p,m)=1, a Sylow p-subgroup is of order p^n and letting n_p be the number of Sylow p-subgroups: (a) n_p ≡ 1 (mod p) and n_p ≠ 0 (existence); (b) n_p divides m; (c) any two Sylow p-subgroups are conjugate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: Sylow p-subgroup is normal iff n_p = 1; use congruence and divisibility to restrict possibilities for n_p and classify groups in many cases. Proof uses group actions (conjugation) and counting orbits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof machinery for Sylow theorems via group actions (Sections 17.2.ii–v)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stepwise proof: Step 1 existence by action on pn-sized subsets (use combinatorial divisibility facts like Lucas theorem to pick orbit size not divisible by p). Step 2 conjugacy by action of Q on left cosets of P. Step 3 congruence n_p ≡ 1 (mod p) by P acting on set of Sylow p-subgroups and counting fixed points. Step 4 n_p divides m by orbit-stabilizer on conjugation action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each step uses the orbit-stabilizer principle and properties of p-groups (orbits sizes are powers of p). The text gives a constructive/probabilistic flavor and highlights how counting arguments yield structural group information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition: triple product of distinct primes implies a normal Sylow subgroup (Proposition 17.1.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If |G| = p q r with distinct primes p < q < r, then G has a normal Sylow subgroup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counting argument: assume all n_p,n_q,n_r > 1 and derive contradiction by counting non-identity elements contributed by Sylow subgroups; uses Lagrange's theorem and intersection size = 1 for different prime-power Sylow subgroups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjugation action on subgroups and normalizer (Definitions 17.2.1 and 17.2.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: G acts on the set X of subgroups by H ↦ g H g^{-1}. The normalizer N_G(H) = {g ∈ G | g H g^{-1} = H} is the stabilizer of H under this action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Properties: conjugate subgroups are isomorphic; normalizer contains H and is used in Sylow arguments (e.g., to show uniqueness of fixed Sylow subgroup under conjugation action).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions and results about simple groups, composition series, and Jordan-Hölder (Section 17.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: A simple group has no nontrivial normal subgroups. A composition series is a maximal chain {1} = H0 ⊴ H1 ⊴ ... ⊴ Hn = G; composition factors Hi/Hi-1 are simple. Jordan-Hölder theorem: composition series are unique up to order of composition factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: composition series of Z/12Z correspond to prime factorizations (illustrated). The section sketches the classification flavors of finite simple groups and notes the exceptional sporadic groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selected advanced problems and theorems to work toward
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems include Cauchy's theorem (existence of element of order p), class equation (Problem 16D), Burnside proof, Engel/word problems, and others probing deeper structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These problems serve as milestones to test understanding and to apply the preceding definitions/theorems; some are marked harder (⋆ or †) and are intended as substantial exercises.
